To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the HASY dataset is a publicly available dataset of handwritten symbols that is suitable for the evaluation of recognition systems for handwritten symbols; 2) the HASY classification challenge has been solved by a deep convolutional neural network with an accuracy of 99.5%, which is a new state of the art;
the classification accuracy on the HASYv2 data set is 97.8% and the verification accuracy is 98.8% (see Section 6).
HASY is a challenging and useful benchmark dataset that can be used for the development of symbol recognition systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how well the HASY dataset can be used to train a classifier that can distinguish between the 369 different classes.
the following questions: (i) How can the performance of the best available methods on HASY be compared with the performance of these methods on the MNIST dataset?

the following questions: How to create a large dataset of handwritten symbols? What are the properties of the HASY dataset? How to train a neural network to recognize symbols from HASY? How to evaluate a neural network trained on HASY? What are the results for different neural network architectures? What are the limitations of the HASY? How is HASY related to other datasets?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HASY dataset is a valuable and challenging dataset for research and development of symbol recognition.
HASY is a challenging dataset for symbol classification and verification.
HASY is a good benchmark for the recognition of handwritten symbols.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HASY is a new benchmark dataset for handwritten symbols.
we provide a new benchmark for symbol recognition, which is a task with a high potential for future research and application in the field of machine vision.
the HASY dataset has been created and is now available for the scientific community.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HASY dataset is suitable to train and test state of the art neural networks for symbol recognition and that it can serve as a test bed for future developments in this field.
the dataset can be used to train a neural network to classify handwritten symbols with a state of the art accuracy of 99.8% on the training and 99.6% on the test set.
the HASY dataset can serve as a good benchmark for the evaluation of handwritten symbol recognition algorithms.
